title: Selling what you do not own
objectives: Compute the profit and the risk of a short sale.

screens.prose: You expect a share now at £50.00 to fall. You borrow one share from a broker and sell it for £50.00. A month later you buy one back at £42.00 and return it to the broker.
screens.question: What is your profit, before any costs?

hints.text: You received cash first and paid cash later. Which was more?
You sold for £50.00 and bought back for £42.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take what you paid to buy back from what you sold for.

byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. Selling high and buying back low is a gain.
byKey.buy: That is what you paid to buy back. Your profit is what you sold for minus that.
byKey.sale: That is the cash from the sale. You still had to buy a share back to return it.

explain.text: You sold first at £50.00 and bought back later at £42.00, keeping £8.00. The line slopes down: you gain £1.00 for every £1.00 the share falls. That is the long share's line, flipped.

screens.prose: Slide the buy-back price across the whole range, from £0.00 to £120.00. Watch the dot's label. Where does the profit stop growing, and where does the loss stop?
screens.question: What is the most this trade can make?

options.text: £50.00, if the share goes to zero
No limit: the further the share falls, the more you make
options.why: You mirrored the long's gains. A price cannot go below £0.00, so the gain stops at the £50.00 you sold for.
That was one outcome. Slide the price to £0.00 and read the label.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price to £0.00 and read the profit.

explain.text: If the company fails and the share goes to £0.00, you buy back for nothing and keep the £50.00. That is the most a short can make. On the right the line keeps falling: at £120.00 you have lost £70.00, and higher prices lose more.

screens.prose: This is a **short sale**. Buying back is **covering** the short. The broker lends you the share for a **stock loan fee**. While you are short, the company pays a £0.60 dividend on each share.

rows: a promise: one share back, and its dividends
£50.00 cash and a debt of one share

screens.question: Who pays the £0.60 dividend to the lender?

options.why: The company pays whoever holds the share now: the buyer you sold to. The lender gets nothing from it, so you must pay.
The buyer owns the share outright and keeps the dividend. The buyer owes the lender nothing.

options.text: Nobody: the lender gave up the share
options.why: The lender only lent the share, and expects every dividend it would have had.

hints.text: The company pays one dividend per share. Who holds the share now?
The buyer holds it and receives the company's dividend.
The lender still expects a dividend, and only you owe the lender anything.

feedback.correct: You pay the dividend to the lender, out of your own pocket.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the share: who holds it, and who is owed?

byKey.company: You assumed the company pays the lender. It pays only the holder, the buyer, so the lender's dividend comes from you.

explain.text: The company pays the buyer, who now holds the share. The lender still expects its £0.60, and you owe it. So a dividend is a cost of being short, on top of the fee.

screens.prose: You short 1,000 shares at £50.00 for three months, then cover at £42.00. The stock loan fee is 3% a year on the £50,000.00 sale value. A £0.60 dividend is paid on each share while you are short.
screens.question: Fill in the cash flows, with money paid out as negative.

hints.text: The fee is a yearly rate charged for a quarter of a year.
Fee: $50{,}000 \times 0.03 \times 0.25$. Dividend: $1{,}000 \times 0.60$.

feedback.correct: £8,000.00 from the price, less £975.00 of costs: £7,025.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill each cost, then add the column.

byKey.r1c1: The fee is 3% a year, but you are short for only a quarter: $50{,}000 \times 0.03 \times 0.25$.
byKey.r2c1: You owe the lender the dividend on all 1,000 shares: $1{,}000 \times \text{£}0.60$, paid out.
byKey.r3c1: Buying back 1,000 shares at £42.00 costs £42,000.00, paid out.
byKey.r4c1: Add the column. Did you forget the dividend you pay the lender?

explain.text: The fall earns $1{,}000 \times (50 - 42) = \text{£}8{,}000.00$. The fee takes £375.00 and the dividend £600.00, leaving £7,025.00. Costs always count against a short, whichever way the share moves.

screens.prose: Same trade, same £375.00 fee and £600.00 of dividends. This time the share rises to £65.00 before you cover.
screens.question: What is your profit? Use a negative number for a loss.

hints.text: Start from the price move, then take off the costs.
The price move costs $1{,}000 \times (65 - 50) = 15{,}000$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The price move loses money, and the costs add to the loss.

byKey.no-costs: You left out the fee and the dividend. They are due whatever the share does.
byKey.costs-helped: You took the costs off the loss. Costs always make a short worse.
byKey.sign: The share rose against you, so this is a loss: use a negative number.

explain.text: Buying back at £65.00 costs £15,000.00 more than the sale raised. The fee and the dividend add £975.00 to the loss. A short pays carry every day it is open, so slow-moving shorts bleed.

screens.prose: A colleague says a short is the mirror of buying: just as a buyer can lose at most £50.00 a share, so can you. You short one share at £50.00. Then the share triples to £150.00.
screens.question: What do you lose on the share when you cover at £150.00, before costs?

hints.text: What must you pay to return the share?
You sold at £50.00 and must buy back at £150.00.
$150 - 50 = 100$: the loss is £100.00, twice what the sale raised.

feedback.correct: You buy back at £150.00 what you sold at £50.00: a £100.00 loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The loss is the buy-back price minus the sale price.

byKey.capped: You capped the loss at the sale price, as for a long. A short must buy back at any price, so the loss has no ceiling.
byKey.whole: You counted the whole buy-back price. The £50.00 from the sale offsets part of it.
byKey.signed: The question asks for the size of the loss, as a positive number.

explain.text: You must buy back at £150.00 a share you sold for £50.00: a loss of £100.00. A price has no ceiling, so the line has no floor. A buyer can lose at most what was paid; a short seller's loss is unlimited.

screens.prose: You sold at $P_0$, covered at $P_1$, and paid fees and dividends $C$: $$\text{profit} = P_0 - P_1 - C.$$ The best case is $P_1 = 0$, a profit of $P_0 - C$. There is no worst case: as $P_1$ rises, the loss grows without limit.
screens.question: You short at £30.00 and cover at £36.00. Fees and dividends come to £0.50 a share. What is your profit per share?

options.why: You took the costs off the loss. Costs always count against you: $30 - 36 - 0.5$.
You subtracted the wrong way round. Covering above the sale price is a loss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the numbers into $P_0 - P_1 - C$.

explain.text: $P_0 - P_1 - C = 30 - 36 - 0.50 = -6.50$. The price move costs £6.00 and the costs add £0.50.

screens.prose: Before you short, your broker must **locate** a share to borrow, and the lender can **recall** it at any time. **Short interest** is the number of shares sold short. In one share, 12 million are sold short and 2 million trade on an average day.
screens.question: How many days of average volume would it take every short seller to buy back?

hints.text: Every short must buy back 12 million shares in total.
The market trades about 2 million a day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the shares sold short by the shares traded a day.

byKey.inverted: You divided volume by short interest. Days to cover is short interest over daily volume.
byKey.product: You multiplied. The shorts need 12 million shares at 2 million a day.
byKey.diff: You subtracted. Divide the short interest by the daily volume.

explain.text: Shorts would need about 6 days of the market's whole volume to cover. If the price jumps, their rush to buy pushes it higher still: a **short squeeze**. In January 2021 GameStop's short interest was about 140% of its freely traded shares, and its price rose more than tenfold in weeks.

screens.prose: A **pairs trade**: long £100,000.00 of one bank's shares, short £100,000.00 of a rival's. Bad news hits the whole sector. The first bank falls 8% and the second 12%.
screens.question: What is the pair's profit, before costs?

hints.text: Work out each leg's profit separately.
The long loses 8% of £100,000.00; the short gains 12% of £100,000.00.

feedback.correct: The long loses £8,000.00, the short gains £12,000.00: £4,000.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A short gains when its share falls.

byKey.both-long: You treated both legs as long. The short leg gains when bank B falls.
byKey.sign: You swapped the legs. The short is in bank B, which fell further.
byKey.zero: Zero net exposure cancels the sector's common move, not the gap between the two shares.

explain.text: The long loses £8,000.00 and the short gains £12,000.00, so the pair makes £4,000.00. With zero net exposure, the shared fall cancels; the trade bets only that A beats B. Its gross exposure is still £200,000.00, which is what that bet is sized on.

screens.prose: A fund shorts 1,000 shares at £100.00, £100,000.00 in all. The stock is hard to borrow, and the fee for the period is £2,000.00. A squeeze lifts the share 50% to £150.00, and the lender recalls it, so the fund must cover.
screens.question: What is the fund's profit, including the fee? Use a negative number for a loss.

hints.text: The fund sold for £100,000.00. What does buying back cost?
Buying back 1,000 shares at £150.00 costs £150,000.00.

feedback.correct: A £50,000.00 loss on the price plus the £2,000.00 fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sale proceeds minus the buy-back cost minus the fee.

byKey.no-fee: You left out the £2,000.00 fee. It is due whatever the share does.
byKey.whole: You counted the whole buy-back as lost. The £100,000.00 from the sale pays for most of it.
byKey.capped: You capped the loss at the sale value. The loss is set by the buy-back price, which has no ceiling.
byKey.sign: The share rose against the short, so this is a loss.

explain.text: Covering costs £150,000.00 against £100,000.00 raised, a £50,000.00 loss, and the fee adds £2,000.00. The recall forced the fund to buy at the top, when it might have waited. Crowded shorts are risky because everyone may need to buy at once.

ideas: A short sale borrows a share, sells it, buys it back later and returns it: profit $P_0 - P_1$ less costs.
The short pays the stock loan fee and every dividend the lender would have had.
The best case is the share going to zero, a profit of $P_0$. The loss has no limit, and recalls and squeezes can force a cover.

formula.name: Short sale profit
formula.note: $C$ is the fee plus the dividends paid to the lender.

summary.trap: The most a short can lose is not the sale price. The share can rise without limit, and you must buy it back.

quiz.prose: You short 200 shares at £25.00 and cover at £20.00. The stock loan fee for the period is £15.00, and no dividend is paid.
quiz.question: What is your profit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gain on the price, then take off the fee.

byKey.per: That is the gain per share. You shorted 200.
byKey.plus: You added the fee. It is a cost of borrowing the shares.

explain.text: The price fall earns $200 \times (25 - 20) = \text{£}1{,}000.00$, and the fee takes £15.00. The profit is £985.00.

quiz.question: What is the most you could lose on it?

options.why: You treated the short like a purchase. A buyer can lose £40.00 at most; you must buy back at any price.
Doubling is one outcome. The share can rise further, and your loss with it.
The fee is a cost, but the main risk is the price rising.

feedback.correct: A share's price has no ceiling, so neither has the loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what you pay to buy back if the share keeps rising.

explain.text: The loss is the buy-back price minus £40.00, plus costs. The buy-back price can rise without limit, so the loss can too.

quiz.prose: You short 500 shares at £40.00. While you are short the company pays a £1.00 dividend per share. The fee is £50.00, and you cover at £40.00.
quiz.question: What is your profit? Use a negative number for a loss.

feedback.correct: No price gain, minus £500.00 of dividends and £50.00 of fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The price did not move, so only the costs remain.

byKey.no-div: You forgot the dividend. You owe the lender £1.00 on each of the 500 shares.
byKey.div-gain: You treated the dividend as income. The buyer receives it; you pay the lender the same amount.
byKey.zero: The price is unchanged, but the fee and the dividend are still due.

explain.text: The price is where you sold it, so the move earns nothing. You pay the lender $500 \times \text{£}1.00 = \text{£}500.00$ and the £50.00 fee. The short loses £550.00.

quiz.prose: You short 1,000 shares at £12.00, with no fees or dividends. The company fails and its shares become worthless.
quiz.question: What is your profit?

feedback.correct: You keep the whole £12,000.00 from the sale.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buying back at £0.00 costs nothing.

byKey.per: That is per share. You shorted 1,000.
byKey.double: You can keep only what the sale raised. The share cannot go below £0.00.
byKey.zero: A worthless share is the short's best case: buying back costs nothing.

explain.text: You sold for £12,000.00 and buy back for nothing. That is the most a short can make: the sale value $P_0$ on every share.
